passages.happening:
“Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God. The authorities that exist have been appointed by God” (verse 1). So whoever resists authority opposes what God has set in place, and will bring judgment on himself (verse 2).

“For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad” (verse 3). Do what is right, and you will have the ruler's approval. “For he is God’s servant for your good” (verse 4). But if you do wrong, be afraid, “for he does not carry the sword in vain” (verse 4).

So believers should submit, not only to avoid punishment, “but also as a matter of conscience” (verse 5). “This is also why you pay taxes” (verse 6). “Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due, revenue to whom revenue is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Paul wrote these words to believers in the capital of the empire, about AD 57. The emperor was Nero, still in the early years of his reign. The burning of Rome, and Nero's killing of Christians, came about seven years later. Christian tradition holds that Paul himself died in Rome under Nero.

The believers in Rome had reasons to be careful. Jews had been driven out of the city under Claudius, perhaps around AD 49, and some of them, like Prisca and Aquila, belonged to these churches. A small, new group that met in homes and honoured a crucified Jew as ‘Lord’ could easily look like trouble to the authorities.

Taxes were a live question in the city. The Roman historian Tacitus records that, around this time, the people of Rome complained loudly about the greed of the tax collectors, so that Nero thought of abolishing the indirect taxes, before his advisers talked him out of it.

Paul names two kinds of payment in verse 7. ‘Taxes’ were most likely direct taxes on people and land, paid by subject peoples. ‘Revenue’ was most likely tolls and customs on goods. Jesus had answered a question about taxes: “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Mark 12:17).

‘God's servant’ is a striking title for a pagan ruler. Paul does not say rulers are good or always right. He says their authority is given, and that its purpose is to restrain evil and protect good.
passages.ot:
Israel's Scriptures teach both sides of this. God gives rulers their place: “He removes kings and establishes them” (Daniel 2:21). Wisdom says, “By me kings reign, and rulers enact just laws” (Proverbs 8:15). When Judah was in exile in Babylon, Jeremiah told them, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf” (Jeremiah 29:7).

But the same Scriptures show God's people refusing rulers who command evil. The Hebrew midwives in Egypt were ordered to kill baby boys. “The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live” (Exodus 1:17). Daniel's friends refused to worship the king's statue: “we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up” (Daniel 3:18). Daniel kept praying when the king forbade it, “just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10). In each case they accepted the ruler's power to punish, and still would not obey a command against God.
passages.hard:
What Paul says is plain: believers are to submit to rulers, pay taxes, and give respect, because rulers hold their authority from God. What Paul does not say is that rulers may command anything. The Bible itself sets limits. When the council in Jerusalem forbade the apostles to preach, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Revelation 13 pictures Rome's power turned against God's people as a beast. Paul describes government as it is meant to work: a terror to bad conduct, not to good.

For centuries this passage was misused to demand obedience to unjust rulers and to defend tyranny and slavery. In the 1850s some preachers called it a religious duty to obey a law requiring the return of people who had escaped slavery; others answered that God's law stands higher. In 1985 Christians living under apartheid, a system of enforced racial separation, rejected in the Kairos Document the use of Romans 13 to give that state absolute and divine authority. That use of the passage is wrong, and these notes reject it. The same standard holds for every government.

Christians differ on when disobedience is right. Most hold that believers must refuse a command to do evil, as the apostles did; they differ on whether, and how, to resist an unjust ruler beyond that. They differ too on the state's sword. Pacifists, such as the Anabaptists and their heirs the Mennonites, refuse all violence. The just war tradition, from Augustine to Thomas Aquinas, holds that love of neighbor can require lawful force to protect the innocent, within strict limits. On the death penalty, some read verse 4 as allowing it for the gravest crimes; others hold that the verse does not require it and that it should end. These notes take no side, and Romans does not tell anyone which party or ruler to support.
passages.asks: Paul asks for respect and honest taxes even toward a pagan ruler. Ask how you speak of those who govern you, whoever they are. Then ask where, if anywhere, your loyalty to God would require you to say no, and pray for both your rulers and your own courage.

passages.t: The one debt that stays: love
passages.happening:
“Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (verse 8).

The commandments, “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not covet,” and every other, are summed up in this one: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (verse 9).

“Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the fulfillment of the law” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Paul has just said, ‘Pay everyone what you owe him’. Now he plays on the word. Pay off every debt, he says, except one. The debt of love can never be paid off. You owe it every day, to everyone.

‘Neighbor’ is not only the person next door. In this letter, after chapters 9 to 12, it plainly includes Jew and Gentile, rich and poor, and even an enemy (12:20).

‘Fulfilled the law’ does not mean love replaces God's commands. It means love does what the commands were aiming at. Someone who truly loves will not commit adultery, murder, steal or covet. Love is not less than the law. It is the law's heart.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes four of the Ten Commandments: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14), “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15), and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house” (Exodus 20:17).

The summary comes from Leviticus: “love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). In its setting, this command sits in a chapter about everyday fairness: leaving grain at the edge of the field for the poor, paying workers on time, judging fairly, and not seeking revenge. Jesus named it as the second greatest commandment (Mark 12:31). Paul takes up the same teaching.
passages.asks: ‘Love does no wrong to its neighbor.’ Think of the people you will meet this week. Ask which one you owe love to that you have not been paying. Then pay something on that debt, in a concrete act.

passages.t: ‘The night is nearly over’: put on Christ
passages.happening:
“And do this, understanding the occasion. The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed” (verse 11).

“The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near. So let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light” (verse 12).

“Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy” (verse 13).

“Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Paul pictures the world's history as one long night, nearly over. The light of a new day is already showing. That day is the return of Christ and the full salvation of God's people. Believers are like people who must get up and dress before the sun is fully up.

The list in verse 13 is what happened at night in a city like Rome: drinking parties, sexual adventures, brawls. ‘Carousing’ means wild, drunken partying. ‘Debauchery’ means living without any restraint. Notice that the list ends with quarrelling and jealousy. Paul puts the church's own quarrels beside drunkenness. The next chapter is about exactly that.

‘Clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ’ is a picture of getting dressed. Paul uses it elsewhere of baptism: “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Believers put on Christ's way of life as one puts on clothes for the day.

‘Make no provision’ means do not plan ahead for sin. Do not leave the door open.

These two verses changed a life. In 386 Augustine, a brilliant teacher who had long resisted the faith, sat in a garden in Milan in deep distress. In his Confessions he tells how he heard a child's voice repeating, as he understood it, ‘take up and read’. He opened Paul's letters and read the first lines his eyes fell on, Romans 13:13-14. He became a Christian.
passages.ot:
The picture of night giving way to day is drawn from the prophets. Isaiah calls, “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you” (Isaiah 60:1).

‘The armor of light’ recalls Isaiah's picture of God himself dressing for battle to save his people: “He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head” (Isaiah 59:17). Paul uses the same picture at length in Ephesians 6.

Readers have also heard in ‘salvation is nearer’ the prophets' hope of a coming day of the LORD, which the New Testament connects with Christ's return.
passages.hard: Paul says ‘the day has drawn near’. Did he expect Christ to return within his own lifetime? Readers differ. Some think Paul did expect the end soon and was not concerned to be precise about time. Others note that Paul never sets a date, and that ‘near’ in the New Testament often means that the next great event in God's plan is the return of Christ, whenever it comes, so believers must always be ready. Christians have long agreed on what Paul asks here, whatever the timing: live now as people of the coming day. These notes do not choose between the readings.
passages.asks: Paul tells believers to get dressed for the day. Name one ‘deed of darkness’ you are tempted to plan for, and close the door on it today. Then read verse 14 and ask what it would look like to put on Christ before you go out.
